en nationalpark.explanation: "En nationalpark" means "a national park". It is built from "national" (national) and "en park" (a park). To say a place is Denmark's first one, say: "Nationalpark Thy var Danmarks første nationalpark" (Nationalpark Thy was Denmark's first national park).

en natklub.explanation: "En natklub" means "a nightclub". It is built from "nat" (night) and "en klub" (a club). The same "nat" is in "en natkjole" (a nightgown).

en natlampe.explanation: "En natlampe" means "a bedside lamp". It is built from "nat" (night) and "en lampe" (a lamp). The same "nat" is in "en natkjole" (a nightgown).

en nattesøvn.explanation: "En nattesøvn" means "a night's sleep". To say you need a good night's sleep, put "god" (good) in front: "Jeg trænger til en god nattesøvn" (I need a good night's sleep).

en naturkatastrofe.explanation: "En naturkatastrofe" means "a natural disaster". It is built from "natur" (nature) and "en katastrofe" (a disaster). To say a place was hit by one, say: "Området blev ramt af en naturkatastrofe" (The area was hit by a natural disaster).

en naturvejleder.explanation: "En naturvejleder" means "a nature guide". It is built from "natur" (nature) and "en vejleder" (an adviser). To say you go on a walk led by one, say: "Vi går en tur med en naturvejleder" (We go for a walk with a nature guide).

en navle.explanation: "En navle" means "a navel". The same "navle" is the start of "en navlestreng" (an umbilical cord). Do not mix it up with "et nav" (a hub), the middle part of a wheel: "Hjulet har et nav" (The wheel has a hub).

en navngivning.explanation: "En navngivning" means "a naming". It comes from the verb "at navngive" (to name). To talk about naming a baby, say: "navngivningen af barnet" (the naming of the child).

en nederdel.explanation: "En nederdel" means "a skirt". It is built from "neder" (down) and "en del" (a part), so it literally means "a lower part".

en nedgang.explanation: "En nedgang" means "a decline". To say an amount went down, use "i" (in) after it: "en nedgang i priserne" (a decline in prices). When you talk about a way down to a lower place, it means "a way down": "Nedgangen til metroen er her" (The way down to the metro is here).

en nedskæring.explanation: "En nedskæring" means "a cutback". It comes from "at skære ned" (to cut back). To say cutbacks are carried out, use "at gennemføre" (to carry out): "Kommunen gennemfører nedskæringer på skolerne" (The municipality is carrying out cutbacks at the schools).

en negl.explanation: "En negl" means "a nail", as in the nail on a finger or toe. To talk about a nail you hit with a hammer, use "et søm" (a nail): "Jeg slår et søm i væggen" (I hammer a nail into the wall).

en neglesalon.explanation: "En neglesalon" means "a nail salon". It is built from "negle" (nails) and "en salon" (a salon). To say you are going there to get your nails done, say: "Jeg skal have lavet negle" (I am getting my nails done).

en nerve.explanation: "En nerve" means "a nerve". To say something annoys you, use "at gå én på nerverne" (to get on someone's nerves): "Støjen går mig på nerverne" (The noise gets on my nerves).

en nevø.explanation: "En nevø" means "a nephew". To say a niece instead, use "en niece" (a niece): "Min niece er fem år" (My niece is five years old).

en niece.explanation: "En niece" means "a niece". To say a nephew instead, use "en nevø" (a nephew): "Min nevø er syv år" (My nephew is seven years old).

en nisse.explanation: "En nisse" means "a Christmas elf". In Danish folklore, "nissen" is a small creature in a red cap who plays tricks if people do not treat him well. At Christmas, Danish children put out "risengrød" (rice porridge) for him.

en nordmand.explanation: "En nordmand" means "a Norwegian". It is built from "nord" (north) and "en mand" (a man). To name the country, use "Norge" (Norway): "Han kommer fra Norge" (He comes from Norway).

en norm.explanation: "En norm" means "a norm". To say something is the normal way to behave, use "normen" (the norm): "Det er normen, at man siger tak for mad" (It is the norm to say thanks for the food).

en note.explanation: "En note" means "a note". To say you write things down while someone speaks, use "at tage noter" (to take notes): "Jeg tager noter i timen" (I take notes in class).

en notesbog.explanation: "En notesbog" means "a notebook". It ends in "bog" (book), like "en ordbog" (a dictionary) and "en lærebog" (a textbook).

en novelle.explanation: "En novelle" means "a short story". To say someone has written one, say: "Hun har skrevet en novelle om sin barndom" (She has written a short story about her childhood). Do not mix it up with "en roman" (a novel), a long book: "Romanen har 400 sider" (The novel has 400 pages).

en nuance.explanation: "En nuance" means "a nuance". When you talk about color, it means "a shade": "en nuance af blå" (a shade of blue).

en nummerplade.explanation: "En nummerplade" means "a license plate". It is built from "nummer" (number) and "en plade" (a plate). "Plade" also means "record", as in "en vinylplade" (a vinyl record).

en nyhed.explanation: "En nyhed" means "a piece of news". To talk about one item of news, say: "Det er en dårlig nyhed" (That is bad news). To talk about the news on TV or radio, use "nyhederne" (the news): "Nyhederne begynder nu" (The news is starting now).

en nyhedsside.explanation: "En nyhedsside" means "a news site". It is built from "nyhed" (a piece of news) and "en side" (a page or a site). To talk about one page in a printed newspaper, use "en avisside" (a newspaper page): "Jeg læser en avisside" (I am reading a newspaper page).

en nyhedsudsendelse.explanation: "En nyhedsudsendelse" means "a news broadcast". It is built from "nyhed" (a piece of news) and "en udsendelse" (a broadcast). To say you watch it in the evening, say: "Jeg ser nyhedsudsendelsen om aftenen" (I watch the news broadcast in the evening).

en nyhedsvært.explanation: "En nyhedsvært" means "a news anchor". It is built from "nyhed" (a piece of news) and "en vært" (a host). When you talk about the host of a party, use "vært" alone: "Værten byder gæsterne velkommen" (The host welcomes the guests).

en nyre.explanation: "En nyre" means "a kidney". The same "nyre" is in "en nyresten" (a kidney stone). To say someone gave a kidney to another person, say: "Han har doneret en nyre til sin bror" (He has donated a kidney to his brother).

en nytårskur.explanation: "En nytårskur" means "a New Year's reception". It is a Danish custom for a company or an organization to invite guests to one in early January, with drinks and short talks, to wish each other a happy new year.

en nål.explanation: "En nål" means "a needle". A very common pair is "nål og tråd" (needle and thread): "Kan jeg låne nål og tråd?" (Can I borrow a needle and thread?).

en næse.explanation: "En næse" means "a nose". To say someone has a good feel for something, use "at have næse for noget" (literally, to have a nose for something): "Hun har næse for gode tilbud" (She has a nose for good deals).

en næsespray.explanation: "En næsespray" means "a nasal spray". It is built from "næse" (nose) and "en spray" (a spray). The same "spray" is in "en hårspray" (a hairspray).

en nød.explanation: "En nød" means "a nut". When you talk about being in danger or great need, it also means "distress": "Han er i nød" (He is in distress).

en nøddeallergi.explanation: "En nøddeallergi" means "a nut allergy". It is built from "nødder" (nuts) and "en allergi" (an allergy). To read the warning on a food package, look for: "Kan indeholde spor af nødder" (May contain traces of nuts).

en nødsituation.explanation: "En nødsituation" means "an emergency". It is built from "nød" (distress) and "en situation" (a situation). The same "nød" is in "en nødudgang" (an emergency exit) and "et nødopkald" (an emergency call).

en nødudgang.explanation: "En nødudgang" means "an emergency exit". It is built from "nød" (distress) and "en udgang" (an exit). To tell people where to go in danger, say: "Brug nødudgangen" (Use the emergency exit).

en nødvendighed.explanation: "En nødvendighed" means "a necessity". It comes from the adjective "nødvendig" (necessary). To say something is necessary, use "nødvendigt": "Det er nødvendigt at have pas" (It is necessary to have a passport).

en nøgle.explanation: "En nøgle" means "a key". To say which door a key belongs to, use "til" (to) after it: "nøglen til din lejlighed" (the key to your apartment).

en nøglering.explanation: "En nøglering" means "a key ring". It is built from "nøgle" (key) and "en ring" (a ring). To say you have lost it, say: "Jeg har mistet min nøglering" (I have lost my key ring).

en nørd.explanation: "En nørd" means "a nerd". To say what someone is a nerd about, put the topic in front in one word: "en computernørd" (a computer nerd) and "en filmnørd" (a movie nerd).

et nabolag.explanation: "Et nabolag" means "a neighborhood". It comes from "en nabo" (a neighbor). To say what kind of people live close to you, say: "Der bor mange børnefamilier i vores nabolag" (Many families with children live in our neighborhood).

et naboskab.explanation: "Et naboskab" means "a neighborhood relationship". The ending "-skab" names a relationship, as in "et venskab" (a friendship). The people themselves are "naboer" (neighbors): "Mine naboer er søde" (My neighbors are nice).

et natbord.explanation: "Et natbord" means "a nightstand". It is built from "nat" (night) and "et bord" (a table). The same "bord" is in "et skrivebord" (a desk) and "et spisebord" (a dining table).

et naturområde.explanation: "Et naturområde" means "a nature area". It is built from "natur" (nature) and "et område" (an area). The same "område" is in "et boligområde" (a residential area) and "et industriområde" (an industrial area).

et navn.explanation: "Et navn" means "a name". To ask someone's name, say "Hvad hedder du?" (What is your name?, literally "What are you called?"). To give your own name, say: "Jeg hedder Anna" (My name is Anna).

et navneord.explanation: "Et navneord" means "a noun". It is built from "navn" (name) and "et ord" (a word). Another word for it is "et substantiv" (a noun). Two examples of nouns are "en bil" (a car) and "Anna".

et nedbrud.explanation: "Et nedbrud" means "a crash". It is built from "ned" (down) and "et brud" (a break). The same "brud" is in "et benbrud" (a broken bone).

et nederlag.explanation: "Et nederlag" means "a defeat". To say a team or a person is beaten, use "at lide nederlag" (to suffer defeat): "Danmark led nederlag i finalen" (Denmark suffered defeat in the final).

et net.explanation: "Et net" means "a net". When you talk about the internet, use "nettet" (the net): "Jeg søger på nettet" (I am searching on the internet).

et netværk.explanation: "Et netværk" means "a network". It is built from "et net" (a net) and "et værk" (a work). To say you know many useful people, use "at have et godt netværk" (to have a good network): "Hun har et stort netværk" (She has a large network).

et nik.explanation: "Et nik" means "a nod". The verb is "at nikke" (to nod): "Han nikker til mig" (He nods at me).

et niveau.explanation: "Et niveau" means "a level". To say how advanced a class is, use it for the steps: "Vi har tre niveauer: begynder, mellem og avanceret" (We have three levels: beginner, intermediate and advanced). Spell the ending "-eau", as in the French word.

et nummer.explanation: "Et nummer" means "a number", as in a label such as "et telefonnummer" (a phone number). To count things or give an amount, use "et tal" (a number or figure) instead: "Tre er et ulige tal" (Three is an odd number).

et nyhedsbrev.explanation: "Et nyhedsbrev" means "a newsletter". It is built from "nyhed" (a piece of news) and "et brev" (a letter). To join the list, use "at tilmelde sig" (to sign up): "Jeg vil gerne tilmelde mig nyhedsbrevet" (I would like to sign up for the newsletter). To leave it, use "at afmelde sig fra" (to unsubscribe from): "Jeg afmelder mig fra nyhedsbrevet" (I am unsubscribing from the newsletter).

et nyhedsprogram.explanation: "Et nyhedsprogram" means "a news program". The first part, "nyheds-", comes from "nyhed" (a piece of news). To say you watch one, say: "Jeg ser et nyhedsprogram hver aften" (I watch a news program every evening).

et nys.explanation: "Et nys" means "a sneeze". The verb is "at nyse" (to sneeze): "Jeg skal nyse" (I have to sneeze).

et nytår.explanation: "Et nytår" means "a New Year". It is built from "ny" (new) and "et år" (a year). To wish someone a happy New Year, say: "Godt nytår!" (Happy New Year!) To say you celebrate it, use "at holde nytår" (to celebrate New Year): "Vi holder nytår hos mine forældre" (We celebrate New Year at my parents' place).

et næb.explanation: "Et næb" means "a beak". The phrase "Hold næb!" (Shut up!, literally "Hold beak!") is rude.

et nødopkald.explanation: "Et nødopkald" means "an emergency call". It is built from "nød" (distress) and "et opkald" (a call). In Denmark, the number to call for help is "112".

et nødstilfælde.explanation: "Et nødstilfælde" means "an emergency". It is built from "nød" (distress) and "et tilfælde" (a case). To say what to do if there is an emergency, use "i" (in) before it: "Brug døren i nødstilfælde" (Use the door in an emergency).

et nøglekort.explanation: "Et nøglekort" means "a key card". It is built from "nøgle" (key) and "et kort" (a card). To tell someone how to open the door with it, say: "Hold nøglekortet op til læseren" (Hold the key card up to the reader).

naiv.explanation: "Naiv" means "naive". After "det" (it, that), add "t" to the word: "Det var naivt at tro på ham" (It was naive to believe him).

narkose.explanation: "En narkose" means "anesthesia", as in the deep sleep for an operation. To say a patient is under it, use "i narkose" (under anesthesia). To numb only one spot, use "en lokalbedøvelse" (a local anesthetic): "Tandlægen giver mig lokalbedøvelse" (The dentist gives me a local anesthetic).

narkotika.explanation: "Narkotika" means "narcotics". To say someone takes drugs, use it without an article: "Han tager narkotika" (He takes drugs).

national.explanation: "National" means "national". To say something belongs to one town only, use "lokal" (local): "en lokal avis" (a local paper). With an "et" word, add "t" to "national": "et nationalt symbol" (a national symbol).

nato.explanation: "NATO" means "NATO". Denmark was one of the countries that founded it in 1949. To join it to another word, add a hyphen: "et NATO-møde" (a NATO meeting).

natur.explanation: "Natur" means "nature". It has no article before it. To say you spend time outdoors, say "i naturen" (in nature): "Vi går en tur i naturen" (We go for a walk in nature).

naturgas.explanation: "En naturgas" means "natural gas". It is built from "natur" (nature) and "en gas" (a gas). To say a house is heated with it, say: "Vi fyrer med naturgas" (We heat with natural gas).

naturlig.explanation: "Naturlig" means "natural". To say something is normal and expected, add "t" after "det": "Det er helt naturligt at være nervøs" (It is completely natural to be nervous). To say something comes from the world as it is, not made by people, use it before a plural noun: "naturlige materialer" (natural materials).

naturligvis.explanation: "Naturligvis" means "of course". The ending "-vis" is also in "heldigvis" (luckily). To answer a question with yes, say it as a reply: "Kan du hjælpe?" "Naturligvis!" (Can you help? Of course!)

navnemåde.explanation: "En navnemåde" means "an infinitive". It is built from "et navn" (a name) and "en måde" (a way), because this form only names the action. In Danish it has "at" (to) in front: "at spise" (to eat).

navnlig.explanation: "Navnlig" means "especially". It is built from "navn" (name) and the ending "-lig". To point out one example from a group, say: "Jeg kan lide sport, navnlig fodbold" (I like sports, especially soccer).

ned.explanation: "Ned" means "down". To tell someone to move to a lower place, say: "Kom ned!" (Come down!) To say where a person already is down there, use "nede" (down there): "Han er nede i kælderen" (He is down in the cellar).

nedad.explanation: "Nedad" means "downward". It is built from "ned" (down) and "ad" (along). To say prices are falling, say: "Priserne går nedad" (Prices are going downward).

nedenunder.explanation: "Nedenunder" means "downstairs". It is built from "neden" (below) and "under" (under). To say a room is on the floor above instead, use "ovenpå" (upstairs): "Soveværelset er ovenpå" (The bedroom is upstairs).

nedslående.explanation: "Nedslående" means "disheartening". To describe bad news, use it before the noun: "nedslående nyheder" (disheartening news). To say a person feels low, use "nedtrykt" (downcast): "Hun er nedtrykt" (She is downcast).

nedtrykt.explanation: "Nedtrykt" means "downcast". It is built from "ned" (down) and "trykt" (pressed), so it literally means "pressed down". To say someone seems low in spirit, say: "Hun virker nedtrykt i dag" (She seems downcast today).

negativ.explanation: "Negativ" means "negative". To say a medical test found nothing, use it for the result: "Testen var negativ" (The test was negative).

neglelak.explanation: "Neglelak" means "nail polish". It is built from "negle" (nails) and "en lak" (a lacquer). To take it off, you need "neglelakfjerner" (nail polish remover): "Har du neglelakfjerner?" (Do you have nail polish remover?)

nej.explanation: "Nej" means "no". When you are surprised or impressed, it also means "oh!": "Nej, hvor er det flot!" (Oh, how beautiful!) To answer yes to a question with "ikke" (not), say "jo" (yes) instead of "ja": "Kan du ikke komme?" "Jo, det kan jeg." (Can't you come? Yes, I can.)

nem.explanation: "Nem" means "easy". To say something is easy to do, use "nem at" (easy to) before the verb: "Appen er nem at bruge" (The app is easy to use). To say a task is hard instead, use "svær" (hard): "en svær opgave" (a hard task).

nemlig.explanation: "Nemlig" means "exactly". To agree with someone, say it as a reply: "Er du træt?" "Nemlig!" (Are you tired? Exactly!) When you give a reason inside a sentence, it means "you see": "Jeg bliver hjemme, jeg er nemlig syg" (I am staying home, I am sick, you see).

nemt.explanation: "Nemt" means "easy". To say how something is done, it means "easily": "Han vinder nemt" (He wins easily). With an "en" word, use "nem" instead: "en nem opgave" (an easy task).

nervepirrende.explanation: "Nervepirrende" means "nerve-wracking". It is built from "en nerve" (a nerve) and "pirrende" (irritating). To describe a movie that makes you tense, say: "en nervepirrende film" (a nerve-wracking movie).

nervøs.explanation: "Nervøs" means "nervous". To say you feel it before something important, say: "Jeg er nervøs før eksamen" (I am nervous before the exam). To say someone is calm instead, use "rolig" (calm): "Hun er helt rolig" (She is completely calm).

nervøsitet.explanation: "En nervøsitet" means "a nervousness". It comes from "nervøs" (nervous). The ending "-itet" is also in "en aktivitet" (an activity). To say someone showed none, say: "Han viste ingen nervøsitet" (He showed no nervousness).

netop.explanation: "Netop" means "exactly". To agree with exactly what someone said, say it as a reply: "Netop!" (Exactly!) To say something happened a moment ago, it means "just": "Han er netop gået" (He just left).

neutral.explanation: "Neutral" means "neutral". To say a country takes no side in a conflict, say: "et neutralt land" (a neutral country). To say a color goes with everything, such as gray, say: "en neutral farve" (a neutral color).

ni.explanation: "Ni" means "nine". The same "ni" starts "nitten" (nineteen) and "niende" (ninth). To say a multiplication, say: "Tre gange ni er syvogtyve" (Three times nine is twenty-seven).

niende.explanation: "Niende" means "ninth". To put things in order, use it after "den" (the): "den niende dag" (the ninth day). To say a date, use it before the month: "den niende maj" (the ninth of May).

nitten.explanation: "Nitten" means "nineteen". To say how much money you have, say: "Jeg har nitten kroner" (I have nineteen kroner).

nogen.explanation: "Nogen" means "anyone". To say you see a person, it means "someone": "Jeg ser nogen" (I see someone). In a question, or after "ikke" (not), it also means "any": "Har du nogen børn?" (Do you have any children?)

nogenlunde.explanation: "Nogenlunde" means "reasonably". To answer "How is it going?" with "so-so", say it as a reply: "Hvordan går det?" "Nogenlunde." (How is it going? So-so.)

nogensinde.explanation: "Nogensinde" means "ever". To ask about your whole life, use it in a question: "Har du nogensinde været i Paris?" (Have you ever been to Paris?) To say never, use "aldrig" (never): "Jeg har aldrig været i Paris" (I have never been to Paris).

noget.explanation: "Noget" means "something". To say you see a thing, say: "Jeg ser noget" (I see something). To say you see a person, use "nogen" (someone): "Jeg ser nogen" (I see someone). Before something you cannot count one by one, such as milk, it means "some": "noget mælk" (some milk).

nogle.explanation: "Nogle" means "some", and it goes with more than one thing: "Jeg har nogle venner" (I have some friends). To talk about one thing, use "en" (a): "Jeg har en ven" (I have one friend). In a question, or after "ikke" (not), use "nogen" (any): "Har du nogen venner?" (Do you have any friends?)

nogle gange.explanation: "Nogle gange" means "sometimes" (literally, "some times"). To say you do something now and then, put it in the sentence: "Jeg spiser nogle gange morgenmad" (I sometimes eat breakfast). To say always, use "altid" (always): "Jeg spiser altid morgenmad" (I always eat breakfast).

nok.explanation: "Nok" means "enough". To say you have enough of something, say: "Jeg har nok mad" (I have enough food). To say what you guess will happen, it means "probably": "Han kommer nok" (He will probably come).

nord.explanation: "Nord" means "north". To say where something is, use "i nord" (in the north): "Skoven ligger i nord" (The forest is in the north). To say which way you are going, use "mod nord" (toward the north): "Vi kører mod nord" (We drive toward the north). The same "nord" is in "Nordjylland" (North Jutland).
